body:
Apax Partners has agreed to sell Tosca , a provider of reusable containers and pallet-pooling services used in food supply chains, to Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Apax first invested in Tosca in 2017.

Tosca rents out and manages the reusable plastic crates, pallets, and bins that carry fresh food from farms and processors to grocery shelves, running them through a pooling model in which customers draw containers as needed and return them to be cleaned and reused rather than buying disposable packaging.Tosca’s assets are used to move eggs, poultry, case-ready meat, seafood, produce, dairy, and beverages, and its customers include growers, food manufacturers, and grocery retailers.

Along with the containers themselves, Tosca operates the wash centers and logistics network that keep them in circulation, cleaning and sanitizing returned assets to food-safety standards, tracking them across customers’ supply chains, and offering a digital ordering platform. The company runs 63 service and wash centers worldwide and serves more than 5,000 customers across 30 countries in North America and Europe. Founded in 1959, Tosca is led by CEO Eric Frank and is headquartered in Atlanta. Goldman Sachs is buying Tosca as an infrastructure asset, framing the company’s pooled containers, wash centers, and customer relationships as essential plumbing of the food supply chain rather than a conventional packaging business.

“Tosca sits at the intersection of several powerful trends, including increased automation in food supply chains, growing demand for circular economy solutions, and the broader adoption of reusable asset pooling,” said Cedric Lucas , a partner within Infrastructure at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. “Its large asset base, integrated service network and best-in-class customer retention underpin its role as essential infrastructure within the food supply chain. We have been highly impressed by the business that Eric and his team have built, and we look forward to partnering with them to support the company’s next phase of expansion.”

“This announcement marks an exciting milestone for Tosca,” said Mr. Frank. “We are grateful for Apax’s partnership and support over the last several years and look forward to working with Goldman Sachs Alternatives as we continue to execute on our strategy. Their long-term investment approach and experience scaling asset-based businesses makes them an excellent partner for the next phase of our growth.”

The global market for reusable transport packaging — the crates, pallets, and bins that pooling companies like Tosca circulate — was valued at about $119.7 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $191 billion by 2033, a compound annual growth rate of roughly 6%, according to Grand View Research . North America is a meaningful share of that total, supported by advanced manufacturing, dense logistics networks, and large grocery and food-distribution operations. Growth is being propelled by retailers and food producers replacing single-use packaging to meet sustainability targets, by the spread of warehouse automation and RFID tracking that pairs well with standardized reusable assets, and by the cost advantages of closed-loop systems over disposable packaging across food, beverage, and pharmaceutical supply chains.

“Tosca provides mission-critical supply chain infrastructure to non-discretionary, resilient staple food end markets,” said Charlotte Saury , a managing director within Infrastructure at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. “Through decades of investments into its network of pooling assets, service centres, and customer relationships, Tosca has established itself as a global leader in reusable asset pooling. We look forward to working alongside Eric and his team to build on this strong foundation through further wash center automation, technology deployment and strategic growth initiatives across North America and Europe.”

Tosca has changed hands several times over the past 15 years. Orchard Holdings , a Cincinnati-based investment firm tied to the founders of Cintas , acquired the company in 2011. Apax bought it in 2017 and expanded it across Europe through two add-on acquisitions: Polymer Logistics , an Israel-based maker of reusable transport packaging and retail-display units (2019), and Contraload , a Belgium-based plastic-pallet-pooling firm (2020).

“We are proud of what Tosca accomplished during our partnership,” said Ashish Karandikar , a partner at Apax. “Working closely with management, we have supported their development into a leading global reusable asset pooling platform with a strong operational foundation and attractive growth prospects. We believe Goldman Sachs Alternatives is the right partner to support Tosca’s next chapter and wish the team continued success.”

The infrastructure business of Goldman Sachs Alternatives has invested about $22 billion in infrastructure assets since it was established in 2006, across digital infrastructure, energy transition, transportation, logistics, and the circular economy. It sits within Goldman Sachs Alternatives, the alternative-investing arm of Goldman Sachs, which has set a target of managing $750 billion in alternative assets by 2030.

Apax is a global private equity firm that has raised and advised on funds with approximately $80 billion in total capital commitments. The firm invests in technology, services, and internet and consumer businesses, and is currently investing from its eleventh buyout fund, Apax XI, which held its final close in March 2024 with more than $12 billion of capital. Apax is headquartered in London with offices across Europe, the Americas, Asia, and the Middle East.

BofA Securities and Goldman Sachs were the financial advisors to Goldman Sachs Alternatives, and Deutsche Bank Securities and William Blair were the financial advisors to Apax.
